lesson.title: End Systems: Where the Network Begins and Ends
lesson.summary: Formalizes the host into the precise architectural term end system, defined by its position at the edge of the network in contrast to the switching equipment in the core.
lesson.body:
The previous section introduced the host as any device that originates or receives data on a network. Networking engineers have a more precise, architectural name for this same idea: the end system. An end system is a host viewed in terms of its position in the network's structure, it sits at the very edge, at one of the endpoints of a communication path, rather than somewhere in the middle relaying other people's traffic. Laptops, desktops, smartphones, game consoles, printers, and servers are all end systems. Routers and switches, even though they are indispensable to the network, are not end systems, because their role is to forward data along, not to be its ultimate source or destination.

The word "end" in end system is doing real work. Picture a communication path as a line segment: the two devices at the far tips of that segment, the ones actually running the application that wants to communicate, are the end systems. Everything in between exists purely to carry the conversation from one end to the other. This is why, when networking texts describe the internet's overall shape, they typically say it consists of end systems connected via access networks to a core of switches and routers. The end systems are the reason the network exists in the first place, and the core exists only to serve them.

End systems are also where application software actually runs. Your web browser, your email client, your video game, and a company's web server all execute on end systems. This matters because it draws a clean line between the applications people care about and the infrastructure that makes those applications possible. A router forwards packets, but it typically does not run a web browser or answer email, its job stops at moving data toward its destination as efficiently as possible.

Consider tracing a video call between two friends. Friend A's laptop and Friend B's phone are the two end systems: the call software runs on each of them, and each is the ultimate source and destination of the audio and video data. Every router, cell tower, and switch that the call's data passes through along the way is part of the network's interior, forwarding the traffic without being party to the conversation. If either laptop or phone is turned off, the call cannot happen, but if a single intermediate router along the path fails, the network usually reroutes around it and the call continues, a good illustration of how end systems, not the interior equipment, are what truly matter to the people communicating.

Because end system is the formal term, you will see it used heavily when discussing network architecture and design, while host remains the everyday word for the same concept, especially in the context of addressing and applications, which the next two sections explore through the client and the server, two specific roles that end systems play in most of today's internet traffic.
